lesson_title: How Many Must She Sell Before She Smiles? Cost Accounting
hook_text: Koeksister number 800 pays the rent. Number 801 feeds the family.
clip_script: Auntie Grace sells koeksisters at the taxi rank, ten rand each. Her grandson, doing grade 12, asks the question that decides whether the stand survives winter: Gogo, how many must you sell each month just to cover yourself? Sort her costs by how they behave. Every koeksister eats about five rand of ingredients and packaging — costs that come and go with each one: variable. And every month, sell or starve, the stand rent takes four thousand rand — the cost that arrives like the calendar: fixed. So each ten-rand koeksister, after feeding itself, CONTRIBUTES five rand toward that rent pile. Now one division: four thousand of fixed costs, five rand of contribution — eight hundred koeksisters. Number 800 pays off the rent exactly. Number 801 is the first one that feeds the family. Prove it: eight hundred sold is eight thousand in; ingredients four thousand, rent four thousand — eight thousand out. Zero. That's break-even. And every decision moves the line: syrup prices rise and each one eats six rand — break-even jumps to a thousand. She raises her price to eleven — it falls to about six sixty-seven. A second stand doubles the rent, and doubles the target. One division, and Auntie Grace can test every business decision before she makes it. So can you.
visual_style: A koeksister stand at golden hour; each sold koeksister dropping a five-rand coin onto a rent pile that fills a marked jar, the jar clicking full at 800; levers labelled price, syrup and rent visibly moving a break-even line up and down.
mood: Warm, resourceful, triumphant at the click.
pacing: Gentle setup, rhythmic coin-drop build, sharp division beat, quick lever montage.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run the break-even machine on any factory the paper invents.
